days.title: The Honest Court
days.place: Astor Courts – Rhinebeck, New York, USA
days.quote: Tennis shows you who you are. Every single day.
days.question: Which three words describe why you play tennis? What draws you to it?
days.journal: Journal: What is your WHY? Why do you get up and train every day? Write down three reasons, the real ones.
text: Tennis has a sound you recognise instantly: the ball skimming low over the net. The short slide in the clay as you reset your feet. The impact that tells you whether you hit the sweet spot.

While other sports bathe in cheering, tennis is a game that listens closely. Two million young people in Germany choose football. About half as many fill tracks and halls with athletics. Tennis remains a smaller world.

Whoever stays here chooses deliberately: precision over mass, responsibility over hiding. On court you stand alone, visible to everyone who is watching. A mistake doesn’t go unheard, and neither does a win.
Every shot makes a statement. Tennis gives you no excuses. And that is exactly what makes it so fascinating, right?
What is the real reason you are here? You chose a game where every contact counts and every decision has an instant echo.
days.umpire: Quiet, please. Advent has begun.

days.title: The Mirror of Your Soul
days.place: Hearst Castle – San Simeon, California, USA
days.quote: Tennis shows you who you are. Every single day.
days.question: What is your biggest goal?
days.journal: Journal: Where do you want to be in one year? Write it down, make it visible.
text: Maybe it is the most honest place you know: a tennis court. You can’t hide here. Your body reveals how you feel. Your eyes show whether you believe you can do it. Your breath shows whether you are centred or fighting.
When you play, everything comes together: your childhood dreams, your ambition, your defiance, your courage. And sometimes your fear of not making it.

There are days when you play with ease. The rhythm is right, you don’t think much, you just feel. And there are days when every ball is a test. Then you get in your own way and realise: the match happens in your head. On hard days you fight against yourself. That is not a flaw in the system. That IS the system.
How do you move when you believe in yourself? How do you talk to yourself when you doubt? What would you tell a friend who is playing the way you are right now?
days.umpire: First serve. No pressure. Okay, a little.

days.title: Your Why
days.quote: Your why carries you when talent is no longer enough.
days.question: What do you play for when nobody is watching? Write one sentence that will still be true in three years.
text: There are days when you play because you have to. And days when you remember why you love it.
Goals help you see the path. But intention shows you why you walk it. Sometimes the two blur into each other. Then you run without noticing where to.
Stop. Not to plan. To feel why you are doing all of this. What was the moment you knew: I really want this? Maybe it wasn’t a win but a feeling. Something that made things clear.
Goals give direction. Intention gives meaning. You need both. But only one carries you when it gets hard.

Your why is the compass when the fog rolls in. When your legs get heavy, your opponent seems stronger, your doubt gets louder. Then you no longer ask yourself “Why am I doing this?” – you already know.
days.umpire: Let! Replay the point – this time with heart.

days.title: Trash Talker
days.quote: The trash talker doesn’t disappear. It is always there. You decide whether you listen.
days.question: Notice three moments today when the trash talker shows up. Stop it. Write down what you thought instead.
text: There is this moment when you know: now it’s getting tight. 30–40, or you just served a double fault. And there it is, that voice in your head – sometimes quiet, sometimes as loud as a megaphone. “Typical. You can’t do this. Why do you even play tournaments?”
There it is again: your inner trash talker. Time to talk back.

Djokovic said: “The biggest battle is always in the mind.” And that is no cliché. Ask Federer how often in his career he had to give himself a kick in the pants because his head was once again faster than his arm.

The nasty part: the trash talker knows your weaknesses. But you can learn to contradict it. Djokovic trains his self-talk like his backhand. Federer sets a positive focus right after a mistake. Alcaraz? Sometimes he simply laughs at himself and thinks: “Okay, that was rubbish, but now more than ever!”
When the trash talker comes, say inside: “Stop!” And replace its sentence with “I learn from every ball” or “The next point is a new chance”.

voice.quote: Sometimes when you force yourself not to think about stuff, the result is the opposite.

days.umpire: Code violation for the trash talker. Unsportsmanlike conduct.

days.title: Training Tunnel Vision
days.quote: Every moment you bring your focus back makes you stronger than yesterday.
days.question: Count how often your focus drifts today. Every return is a mental rep. Goal: 10 conscious returns.
text: Focus is muscle work. You train it like your serve: through repetition.

You know the feeling: the rally is on, and suddenly your eyes drift – to your opponent, to the score, to the spectators. Federer talks about “tunnel vision”: in the decisive moment there is only ball, racket, movement.

But the mind always wants to wander, looks for distraction, especially when things get tight. That is where your job begins: bringing your focus back again and again, like a dog on a lead. Every drifting thought is an invitation to choose again: “Back to the ball. Back to me.”
Focus is not a state you reach once and then keep. Focus is a decision you make a hundred times per match. Every return makes you stronger.

li: “Ball. Racket. Movement. That’s all I need.”

days.umpire: No phones during the rally, please. Except for this app.

days.title: Sensory Anchor
days.place: Hotel Il San Pietro – Positano, Italy
days.quote: Your anchor brings you back when your mind drifts. Choose wisely.
days.question: Choose one sensory anchor for today. Use it at every changeover. How often did it bring you back?
text: You walk onto the court, the air full of expectations, your head full of thoughts.
Jannik Sinner stays present by focusing again and again on one sense: hearing, feeling or seeing.

li: Feel: the grip in your hand
Hear: the rhythmic sound of the ball
See: the lines on the court

text: Presence is not a state. It is a decision: Now. Here. This ball.
When your mind drifts – to the last mistake, the next opponent, the rankings – you bring yourself back. With one single sensation. With every conscious sensation your control grows.
days.umpire: Challenge! Hawk-Eye confirms: you are well in.

days.title: Your Personal Ritual
days.quote: Your ritual is your reset button. Press it on purpose.
days.question: Create your pre-point ritual. Test it ten times today. When did it work, when not?
text: Rituals are mental anchors. They give you control when everything else gets out of control.
Federer bounces the ball the same number of times before every serve. Djokovic bounces, looks, breathes. Sinner adjusts his cap, Alcaraz briefly closes his eyes.

What is behind it? Your brain loves patterns. Under pressure it looks for safety – and rituals deliver exactly that. A ritual is like an anchor that brings you back when your head is on a merry-go-round.

text.h: It doesn’t have to be spectacular
li: one deep breath
a touch of the grip
a sentence only you know
a small movement

days.umpire: You take time for your ritual. Allowed.

teaser.title: Your mental coach
teaser.text: In the Inner Match app you build your own match ritual with your mental coach.

days.title: The 16-Second Rule
days.quote: You don’t win the match with the last point, but always with the next one.
days.question: Use the 16-second routine after every important point today. At which score was it hardest?
text: You just served a double fault. Or hit a winner. Either way: the next point is already knocking.
Now comes the moment most players underestimate: the 16 seconds between rallies.

Federer? Uses them to reset. Djokovic? Breathes deeply, stares into space, shakes off the last point. Alcaraz? Slaps his thighs: “Come on, keep going!” These 16 seconds decide whether you drag the last point along or start fresh.

li: Ritual (3 sec): grip, strings, cap
Breath (5 sec): deep in, slowly out
Focus (5 sec): next point, clear intention
Readiness (3 sec): “I’m ready.”

days.umpire: The shot clock is running. 16 seconds. Breathe.

days.title: Inner Metronome
days.quote: Whoever controls their breath controls their heart. Whoever controls their heart controls the match.
days.question: When did you breathe consciously today? What effect did it have?
text: Your breath is the metronome of your game. When your pulse races, your head buzzes and your legs get heavy, your breath is your anchor. Djokovic swears by breathing exercises to calm down and stay focused in tight matches.
HRV (heart rate variability) measures how flexibly your nervous system responds to stress. High HRV: you are ready. Low HRV: you are running on reserve.
The game changer: you can influence your HRV through your breath. A longer exhale activates your relaxation system. Your body powers down. Your head gets clear.

li: Inhale: 4 seconds (nose)
Hold: 2 seconds
Exhale: 6 seconds (mouth)
Repeat: 3 to 5 times
before the match: 5 minutes
at changeovers: 3 cycles
after mistakes: 1 deep breath
before sleep: 10 minutes

days.umpire: Medical timeout? No. Breathing timeout.

days.title: Changeover Fuel Stop
days.quote: The changeover is your anchor. With this ritual you have everything you need to reset in any match.
days.question: Use 4-2-6 breathing at three changeovers today. How did your pulse change? And your head?
text: You sit on the bench. Just lost a long rally. Pulse pounding. Now the changeover, the moment many underestimate. Not you.
Djokovic uses these breaks as his mental fuel stop. While others are still brooding, you use the 90 seconds to realign.

li: Body (10 sec): racket beside you, 3 deep breaths (4-2-6 from door 9), loosen your shoulders
Reset (10 sec): check the strings, feel the grip
Mind (10 sec): “I’m ready. The next point is mine.” Eyes forward
Readiness (10 sec): stand up, upright body language, “I’m ready.”

text: Important: you decide how you use the break.
days.umpire: Changeover. 90 seconds. Bananas allowed.

days.title: Mastering Self-Talk
days.quote: Your inner dialogue is your most important training partner. Choose it wisely.
days.question: Choose a power sentence: what would you tell yourself in the Wimbledon final? Did it work?
text: Your head is not a loudspeaker for doubt, it is your toolbox.
Self-talk is more than a slogan for motivational posters. It is what you tell yourself in the decisive moment. It becomes your reality. Point by point.

Loehr worked on exactly this with world-class players: not ignoring mistakes, but consciously steering how you talk to yourself in that moment. Self-talk is training, just like your serve and your backhand.

li: Not “I mustn’t make a mistake”, but “I play my shot.”
Not “Just don’t lose now”, but “Every point is new.”

text: Self-talk is like a coach who is always with you. You decide whether it drives you or holds you back. Every champion has their own sentence, their own mantra. What is yours?

voice.quote: Am I the greatest? I don’t know. I’m the greatest that I can be.

days.umpire: Note to the box: only positive talk on this court.

days.title: ABC Analysis
days.quote: Between stimulus and response lies your freedom. Use it.
days.question: Which alternative thought would have changed the point?
text: Between what happens and how you react, there is a space. In that space lies your power. Jannik Sinner describes how he observes his thoughts instead of believing them.
Take a moment from a match that triggered you and go through it like this:

li: A – Activating event: what happened? A missed break point, a service error, an argument with yourself.
B – Belief: what did you tell yourself? “I can’t do this” or “This always happens to me”?
C – Consequence: what followed? Did you withdraw, play more cautiously, or get angry and make even more mistakes?

text: Do you notice how much your evaluation sets the direction? How a single thought can tip everything? But what happens when you question that thought?
With every conscious look at your thoughts, your freedom to react differently grows. The ABC analysis is your key to turning every frustrating moment into a chance to learn.
days.umpire: The call is under review … that thought was out.

days.title: Body Language as a Statement
days.quote: Your body speaks before you think. Control the message.
days.question: Watch your posture after every mistake today. Stand tall. What changed?
text: You stand on the baseline. The sun is burning, the clay sticks to your sweat, your socks stopped being white a long time ago. How you stand now decides how you keep playing.
Federer straightens up after a mistake, chest out, eyes forward. Djokovic pounds his chest, Sinner clenches his fist, Alcaraz grins in the face of pressure.

Body language is intention in action, your statement to yourself before your opponent sees it. Every hanging head, every drooping shoulder feeds doubt. Every upright posture, every firm step says: “I’m still here. And I’m staying.”
Your body often knows how things will go before your head gets it. So: show what you’ve got. Even when it’s hard, especially then. Because sometimes the comeback starts with one single step forward.

voice.quote: I really think a champion is defined not by their wins but by how they can recover when they fall.

days.umpire: Shoulders back. That counts as a point here.

days.title: Mastering Clutch Moments
days.place: Pearl Beach Resort – Bora Bora, French Polynesia
days.quote: Clutch moments are decided not by talent, but by training.
days.question: Simulate three clutch moments in training. Which one worked?
text: There are points that decide everything. Break point against you, set point for you, the last point of a tiebreak. Your heart pounds in your ears, the clay crunches under your shoes, the grip suddenly feels strange.

That is a clutch moment: the instant when pressure is at its highest and you still want to deliver and be fully present. This is where courage separates from routine. Many freeze or hope their opponent will make the mistake. But you can learn to recognise these moments and use them.
Here’s how: you breathe deeply, tell yourself one clear sentence (“Now I’ll show what I can do!”) and focus on your shot. You, the racket and the ball: the trilogy of triumph.
Clutch moments are not a matter of luck. They are your chance to grow. Every time you dare to play your game in the decisive moment, your clutch power grows. Point by point.

voice.quote: Pressure is a privilege and champions adjust.

days.umpire: Break point. The crowd holds its breath. You don’t.

days.title: The Courage to Be Yourself
days.quote: Courage is a muscle. You train it every time you don’t hide.
days.question: Choose three courageous moments. How did you feel afterwards?
text: Courage is rarely loud. Often it begins where you doubt, when you stay even though it gets uncomfortable.

Courage means doing what is right despite fear. On court that means going for the risky winner when it matters. Going all-in again right after a mistake. Playing your game, not the one others expect. Not loud wanting, but quiet going.
Authenticity means you play the way you are, not the way you should be. You stand by your emotions instead of hiding them. You dare not to be perfect at everything yet.
Courage is a muscle. It grows every time you take fear by the hand, or let it chatter away on the bench in the distance.

voice.quote: It’s O.K. to not be O.K.

days.umpire: A miss? Never mind. Courage counts double today.

days.title: Your Perfect Tournament Day
days.quote: Your perfect tournament day: good sleep, perfect preparation. You have all the tools.
days.question: Which phase of your tournament day still needs strengthening?
text: You have a bag full of tools. Now put them together for your perfect tournament day.

li: 10 min: get up, open the window, daylight, silence
20 min: light breakfast (oats, banana, water)
15 min: mental preparation, visualise your goals
30 min: easy warm-up, mobility
10 min: physical activation
10 min: mental focus with breathing exercises
10 min: technical warm-up at the net
16-second rule between points
use your changeover ritual
when in trouble: back to your breath
5 min: wind down consciously
cool-down and stretching
reflection: what went well? What can get better?

days.umpire: Tournament day. Do not disturb, winning in progress.

days.title: Tackling Limiting Beliefs
days.place: Hacienda de la Paz – Rolling Hills, California, USA
days.quote: It’s not your circumstances that limit you, but the stories you tell yourself.
days.question: Take one belief and go through the four steps. How does the new belief feel?
text: These voices run in the background like a bad soundtrack. Time to change the playlist.
“I can’t play under pressure.” “I always make mistakes on big points.” “I’m just not good enough.” Do you know these voices? Those are your limiting beliefs.

li: Identify: which negative beliefs do you hold about yourself?
Question: is it really true? Always? Without exception?
Collect evidence: when did you prove the opposite?
Reframe: which new belief would be more helpful?

text: Example: Old: “I always fail under pressure.” Question: really always? What about last week’s match? New: “I’m learning to give my best under pressure.”
days.umpire: Appeal denied: you are good enough.

days.title: Your Mental First-Aid Kit
days.quote: Your personal toolset is your anchor when everything else is shaking.
days.question: Choose one tool and test it in three pressure situations. When does it work, when not?
text: Every top player has their own emergency kit that gives them support when things get tight. Federer reaches for the towel, Djokovic uses his breathing technique, Sinner straightens up again and again with one conscious movement.
Today it’s your turn: build your mental first-aid kit for difficult moments.

li: a sentence you say to yourself
a small gesture (clench your fist, adjust your cap)
an image in your head that focuses you instantly
a breathing technique (4-2-6 rhythm)
a body movement (roll your shoulders, stand tall)
Identify the situation: when do you need support most?
Choose a tool: what feels right for you?
Test it: try it out consciously.
Adjust it: refine it until it becomes automatic.

text: With every tool you become more independent of external circumstances.
days.umpire: Trainer to the court. Mental plasters only today.

days.title: Sleep Decides Everything
days.quote: Good sleep is the foundation for everything you want to achieve.
days.question: Choose one sleep improvement and test it for three days. How did your energy change?
text: You open the curtains and let the first sunlight fall on your face. Your body wakes up, your head clears, the tiredness fades.
Real daylight in the morning gets your rhythm going and helps you feel genuinely tired in the evening. Sleep is not a luxury. It is the foundation. The day begins before you ever step on court.

li: 7–9 hours of sleep, fixed times
a cool (16–18 °C) and dark room
phone away one hour before bed
morning: 10–15 minutes of direct sunlight
midday: a short break outdoors
evening: dimmed light, avoid blue light
air the room, fresh air
breathe deeply, let the day go
gratitude: three good moments of the day

days.umpire: Lights out. Match day tomorrow. Sleep well.

days.title: Mental Fuel
days.quote: Mental strength needs fuel. Give your brain the best conditions.
days.question: Test it and find out: what refreshes you the most?
text: Mental strength needs fuel, quite literally. Your brain is a high-performance organ: it needs water, vitamins, minerals and healthy fats to stay focused, calm and quick to react.

li: Water: 40 ml per kg of body weight, more when you train
Omega-3 (EPA and DHA): fish, nuts, linseed oil for concentration
Magnesium: against stress and for strong nerves
Vitamin D and B vitamins
5 minutes of fresh air every 2 hours
conscious stretching between study sessions
a glass of water, drunk mindfully
10 deep breaths when stressed

text: Screen rule: screen time is stress for your brain.
days.umpire: Short break. Christmas cookies count as carbs.

days.title: Locker Room Code
days.place: Baile na Cille – Isle of Lewis, Outer Hebrides, Scotland
days.quote: The greats are remembered not only for their wins, but for their attitude. Williams, Federer, Nadal, Djokovic, Sinner, Alcaraz – and one day: you.
days.question: Did you live by your code today? Where were you strong? Where can you improve?
text: There is a difference between a good player and a champion. It isn’t just talent. Not technique. Not the wins. It is the code: the unwritten rules that separate the greats from the good. Federer, Nadal, Djokovic, they all live it. Now it’s your turn.

li: Respect for your opponent
Humility in victory
Dignity in defeat
Taking responsibility
Professionalism
Respect for the team
Consistency

text.h: Tennis is a school for life
li: How do you deal with pressure?
How do you react to defeat?
Who are you when nobody is watching?

text: The code doesn’t just make you a better player. It makes you a better person. It is an attitude. You have to live it. Every day. Every point. Every match.
days.umpire: Handshake at the net. The code demands it.

days.title: Friendship
days.quote: You are not alone on this path. Build a team that carries you.
days.question: Name three people who strengthen you and thank them today. Which boundary do you need with a relationship that drains you?
text: Tennis is an individual sport, but mental strength doesn’t grow alone. Mental strength is also the art of relationships. It lives from honest encounters, from people who want to see you grow, and from spaces where you can simply be yourself.
The people around you – family, friends, coaches, training partners – strengthen you or weaken you.

li: They believe in you, even when you doubt.
They give honest feedback without hurting you.
They celebrate your wins and comfort you after defeats.
They challenge you without overwhelming you.
constant criticism without solutions
comparisons that make you feel small
a negative attitude (“You’ll never make it”)
drama and unnecessary conflict
Say clearly what you need: “Right now I need encouragement, not analysis.”
Set boundaries: “Negative comments before matches don’t help me.”
Say thank you for support.

days.umpire: A round of applause for your team in the box.

days.title: Your Toolbox
days.place: Mauna Kea Beach Hotel – Hawaii, USA
days.quote: Process over progress. Not the perfect day, but getting better every day.
days.question: What are your top 5 tools? When do you use them, and why do they work for you?
text: Mental strength is not a recipe that works the same for everyone. What works for Federer doesn’t have to fit you. What matters is that you keep going, experiment, adjust and keep finding out what really makes you stronger.

li: Which tools from the past weeks worked?
What felt right, what didn’t?
Which techniques do you want to deepen?
What do you still need?
conscious breathing before important presentations
mini rituals when everyday life gets stressful
clear focus when making decisions
positive self-talk in difficult situations
10 minutes of mental training every day
weekly reflection: what went well?
adjust your tools every month

days.umpire: New balls, please. And new tools.

days.title: Your Anchor
days.quote: Your highlights are proof of what is possible when you give everything.
days.question: Choose your strongest moment and relive it: how did you feel? What did you think? How was your posture?
text: You leaf back through your memories: a match that challenged you. A moment when you gave everything. Maybe it was a narrow win, maybe a match you lost – but you grew beyond yourself.

You can still feel the adrenaline, the trembling in your fingers, the clay in your shoe, the laughter after a long rally. These are the moments when you surprised yourself: you hung in there, didn’t give up, showed courage where others would have doubted.

li: Collect moments: which five tennis moments make you proud?
Recognise qualities: what did you show in those moments?
Find patterns: what did those situations have in common?

days.umpire: Game, set and match!

days.title: A Celebration
days.quote: Merry Christmas.
days.question: Travel into the future: choose a date. Where will you be? Who is with you? What are you experiencing? What did you do to get there?
text: Today is a time to celebrate and a time to live miracles. When two people unite behind one purpose, miracles are possible. I am number one, you are number two. Would you have thought this journey was possible? How do you feel? You have given yourself the greatest gift. You are the gift, the miracle.
Pause, be proud, celebrate yourself. You have really rocked this.

And before there are more gifts, I invite you on a journey. One that you shape yourself with your clear intention. A true intention is more than a wish. It runs right through you. It is uncompromising and self-evident, like the child at the supermarket checkout who doesn’t just want a lollipop – it already is the lollipop. Come what may.

Go through the dream courts of the last 24 days once more. Then travel into the future and choose a date. Where will you be? What do you feel? Who is with you? What do you hear, see, smell? How did you get there? Take all of it in. And keep coming back here – back to the future.
And now for my gift: your digital mental coach is waiting for you, always by your side. You are not alone.
days.umpire: Merry Christmas. Game over? No: game on.
